```{=html}
<style>.lx-studio-brief { margin-bottom: 14px; display: grid; gap: 8px; }
#selfcheck .lx-myths { margin-top: 18px; }</style>
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> a design card for one brief: its scale, its <span class="lx-term" data-term="system-boundary">boundary</span> (inside, given, left out), a time step and horizon, a method family, and a defence of that method against two alternatives.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> three illustrative briefs at three scales, each a different type of question.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> your method is defended against two alternatives, one of them a different family, and the scale and boundary are stated.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about an hour on your own: take your own question card from R1 through the same moves, and write a defence of three or four sentences.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r03-system-and-method" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r03-system-and-method.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The moves, in order</p>
<ol>
<li>Place the question on the scale ladder: device and plant, microgrid and community, regional grid, city and region, nation.</li>
<li>Draw its boundary: what the study decides or computes, what it takes as given, and what it leaves out and says so.</li>
<li>Pick a time step that shows what the metric needs, and a horizon that covers the decision.</li>
<li>Choose a method family, then defend it against a simpler version and against another family, and name its main limit.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Three briefs, with a researcher's answers</p>
<!-- r03-task:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Keep the hospital running (prescriptive, S1)</summary>
<p><strong>What sizes of solar, battery and backup generator keep Prairie Campus's hospital supplied through a three-day winter outage at the lowest 20-year cost, compared with today's diesel generator alone?</strong></p><ul>
<li><strong>Scale:</strong> S1: one campus that can run on its own, sized by its owner under the utility's rules. The tariff and the feeder's limits come from the regional grid above.</li>
<li><strong>Inside:</strong> Sizes of solar, battery and generator (These are the decisions the study makes).</li>
<li><strong>Given:</strong> The hospital's critical load, hour by hour (A measured or estimated input; the study does not change it); The utility's tariff and the feeder's export limit (Set at the scale above; fixed inputs here); Hourly winter weather for solar output (An input: a design winter, or several past ones); Diesel fuel stored on site when the outage starts (A fixed limit in the outage case).</li>
<li><strong>Left out:</strong> Wholesale prices across the Plains Grid (The campus pays a tariff, not wholesale prices: say so as a limit); Road access for fuel trucks during the storm (Left out and stated: the design must last three days on stored fuel); Who owns the system and who pays for it (A separate question about ownership, noted as a limit of the cost result).</li>
<li><strong>Time step and horizon:</strong> 1 hour, hourly steps follow solar's daily cycle and the battery's charge; a typical year plus the outage.</li>
<li><strong>Method families:</strong> Optimization: fits well; Simulation: fits well; Statistics and econometrics: helps with a part; Machine learning: poor fit for this question; System dynamics: poor fit for this question; Agent-based modelling: poor fit for this question; Equilibrium modelling: poor fit for this question; Qualitative methods: helps with a part; Mixed methods: fits well.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's defence (Optimization):</strong> I chose a sizing MILP with hourly steps, a typical year plus a three-day outage, over an LP with continuous sizes, because the generator has a minimum load and comes in whole units. I chose it over a simulation of candidate designs, because the question asks for the cheapest mix, not a ranking of mixes I already have. Its main limit is perfect foresight during the outage; I test the chosen design afterwards in a rule-based simulation that does not know the future.</li></ul></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Did the rebate reach low-income homes? (evaluative, S3)</summary>
<p><strong>Did Prairie City's 2023 heat-pump rebate raise installations in its low-income neighbourhoods, compared with similar neighbourhoods in cities without a rebate?</strong></p><ul>
<li><strong>Scale:</strong> S3: a city programme, set by the council with local money and rules. Federal incentives come from the nation above; the homes below act on them.</li>
<li><strong>Inside:</strong> Heat-pump installations per 1,000 homes, by neighbourhood and month (The outcome the study measures); The choice of comparison neighbourhoods (A design decision of the study, and the one that matters most).</li>
<li><strong>Given:</strong> The rebate's rules, amount and start date (Fixed facts of the programme); Neighbourhood income and housing data from the census (Input data, used to match similar neighbourhoods); Federal tax credits available everywhere (The same in every city, so the comparison removes them).</li>
<li><strong>Left out:</strong> Whether the heat pumps lowered bills (A different question, for a later study); Installers' waiting lists (Left out and stated: they may have limited uptake); Grid upgrades for the new heating load (Outside a question about uptake).</li>
<li><strong>Time step and horizon:</strong> 1 month, monthly counts show the change around the rebate's start; 2019 to 2025, before and after.</li>
<li><strong>Method families:</strong> Optimization: poor fit for this question; Simulation: poor fit for this question; Statistics and econometrics: fits well; Machine learning: helps with a part; System dynamics: poor fit for this question; Agent-based modelling: helps with a part; Equilibrium modelling: poor fit for this question; Qualitative methods: helps with a part; Mixed methods: fits well.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's defence (Statistics and econometrics):</strong> I chose a difference-in-differences comparison, with monthly installations by neighbourhood from 2019 to 2025, over a before-and-after count in Prairie City alone, because prices and federal credits changed everywhere at once. I chose it over an agent-based adoption model, because that model would assume how households respond, which is what this study must measure. Its main limit is the assumption that both groups would have moved in parallel without the rebate; I check their trends before 2023 and repeat the comparison with a second group.</li></ul></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>A large load that can pause (predictive, S2)</summary>
<p><strong>How would a 300 MW load that can pause for up to four hours during scarcity change the Plains Grid's expected unserved energy in a heat-wave year, compared with the same load running flat?</strong></p><ul>
<li><strong>Scale:</strong> S2: adequacy belongs to the whole synchronous grid and its operator. The load itself, at the device and plant scale, only decides when it pauses.</li>
<li><strong>Inside:</strong> When the load pauses, hour by hour (Set inside the study by a pausing rule); Random generator outages (Drawn many times by the study, to give a range).</li>
<li><strong>Given:</strong> Hourly demand and weather for a heat-wave year (Input data: a past heat-wave year, or a scaled one); Today's plants and the transfer limits between zones (Fixed: the question asks about the system as it is); Imports from neighbouring grids (Fixed limits, stated).</li>
<li><strong>Left out:</strong> The load's contract: who pays for pausing (A separate question about contracts and tariffs); Voltage and stability in the seconds after a trip (A different time scale, and a different study); New plants built because the load arrived (A planning question; this one keeps the fleet fixed).</li>
<li><strong>Time step and horizon:</strong> 1 hour, adequacy studies count unserved energy hour by hour; one year, run many times.</li>
<li><strong>Method families:</strong> Optimization: helps with a part; Simulation: fits well; Statistics and econometrics: helps with a part; Machine learning: poor fit for this question; System dynamics: poor fit for this question; Agent-based modelling: helps with a part; Equilibrium modelling: poor fit for this question; Qualitative methods: helps with a part; Mixed methods: helps with a part.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's defence (Simulation):</strong> I chose a Monte Carlo adequacy simulation, a heat-wave year with hourly steps run many times, over a check of the single worst hour, because the question asks how often and how much, not only whether. I chose it over a capacity-expansion optimization, because the question keeps today's plants and asks for a risk, not a plan. Its main limit is that outages are drawn independently, while a heat wave can cause several at once; I add a run with linked outages as a sensitivity.</li></ul></details>
<!-- r03-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you make each choice yourself, with a note on how well it fits, and your design stays in this browser.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><span>The briefs, Prairie Campus, Prairie City, the Plains Grid and the 300 MW load are illustrative. The fit notes are teaching judgements, not rules: several method families can answer one question well.</span></p>
```
:::

## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r03-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<p>Defend a method for: “How sensitive is a national storage build-out to a one-year disruption of one mineral, and which design choices reduce the risk?”</p>
<!-- r03-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML, and the method families from the data file, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p>I will use capacity-expansion optimization [1] because it is the standard tool for national planning [2] and it gives the optimal answer [3]. It will cover the whole country [4].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> A family is named, but nothing says why it fits a question about sensitivity and risk.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Chosen by habit: the rubric's Developing anchor for method fit.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> Optimal only inside the model's assumptions, and one run gives no range.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> A scale, but no boundary, time step or horizon.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Strong</p><p>A predictive question at the national scale. I will run a capacity-expansion model (optimization) under many disruption cases drawn at random [1], with yearly steps to 2040 and representative hours inside each year [2]. I chose it over a single run with expected prices [3], which hides the risk the question asks about, and over a system-dynamics model of mineral supply [4], which would capture market feedback but not the grid's hourly needs. Its main limit is perfect foresight inside each case [5]; I reduce it by fixing early builds before the disruption is known.</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Matches the question: “how sensitive” needs a range, not one plan.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> Time step and horizon stated, matched to a build-out over years.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> Alternative one: a simpler version of the same family, rejected for a reason.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> Alternative two, from another family: what the Proficient anchor asks for.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> The limit stated and partly mitigated: the Strong anchor.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Why this family</th><td>Habit</td><td>Tied to the question type</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Time step and horizon</th><td>Not stated</td><td>Yearly to 2040, representative hours</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Alternatives</th><td>None</td><td>One in the family, one from another</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Limit</th><td>None</td><td>Stated, with a way to reduce it</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Nine method families, side by side</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Family</th><th scope="col">Answers</th><th scope="col">Needs</th><th scope="col">Main limit</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Optimization</td><td>What is the best choice under stated rules and goals?</td><td>Decisions, a goal, rules (constraints) and their data.</td><td>Best only inside the model: it takes the stated goal and, usually, perfect foresight.</td></tr><tr><td>Simulation</td><td>What happens when the system runs by given rules, under given conditions?</td><td>Operating rules, inputs over time and the designs to test.</td><td>It tests the designs you give it; it does not search for the best one.</td></tr><tr><td>Statistics and econometrics</td><td>How much, how often, and did a change cause an effect?</td><td>Observed data with variation; for a causal claim, a comparison group.</td><td>It sees only the observed past; causal claims rest on assumptions about the comparison.</td></tr><tr><td>Machine learning</td><td>What will the next value be, or which pattern is this?</td><td>Many examples, honest baselines and data held back for testing.</td><td>It predicts within the range of its training data and explains little about why.</td></tr><tr><td>System dynamics</td><td>How do stocks, flows and feedback shape a trend over years?</td><td>A causal-loop structure and parameters for each flow.</td><td>It works with aggregates, and many parameters rest on judgement.</td></tr><tr><td>Agent-based modelling</td><td>How do many deciding actors produce a system outcome?</td><td>Rules for each kind of actor, and data on how they behave.</td><td>Results depend on behaviour rules that are hard to check against data.</td></tr><tr><td>Equilibrium modelling</td><td>Where do prices and quantities settle when many markets or players interact?</td><td>Supply and demand, market rules and how players respond to prices.</td><td>It describes a settled state, not the path to it, and simplifies how players behave.</td></tr><tr><td>Qualitative methods</td><td>How and why do people and institutions decide as they do?</td><td>Interviews, documents or cases, with consent and a plan for the analysis.</td><td>It gives no numbers that generalise; this course teaches it at awareness level only.</td></tr><tr><td>Mixed methods</td><td>Questions that need both numbers and people's reasons.</td><td>A model or data analysis, a qualitative part, and a plan for how each informs the other.</td><td>More time, and both parts must answer the same question.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<!-- r03-exemplars:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

## Check your own work against the rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r03-rubric" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r03-rubric:start (written by LX.Rubric's staticHTML, from the course rubric, and the scales from the data file, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts lx-rb-static"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Competence</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient (the bar)</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Framing<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: the scale and the boundary are stated, including what is left out.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Question vague or untyped; no audience or counterfactual.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Typed question with audience or decision-maker, metric with units, counterfactual, scale and boundary; one falsification statement.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also explains why the question matters to its audience and what answer would change a decision.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Method fit<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: two alternatives named, one from another family, each rejected for a reason tied to the question.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Method chosen by habit.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Method defended against two alternatives, one of them a different family.</td><td data-l="Strong">Limits of the chosen method stated and partly mitigated.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Five scales: who decides, and typical steps and horizons</p>
<ul><li><b>S0 Device and plant:</b> decides what to install at one site, and how to run it; the owner, within tariffs and codes. Time step: minutes to an hour; horizon: a day to the equipment's life.</li><li><b>S1 Microgrid and community:</b> decides sizes, islanding, load priorities, ownership; a facility owner or co-op, under the utility's rules. Time step: minutes to an hour; horizon: an outage to about 20 years.</li><li><b>S2 Regional grid:</b> decides commitment, dispatch, reserves, transmission, new plants; the grid operator or utility, and regulators. Time step: seconds to an hour; horizon: the next hour to several decades.</li><li><b>S3 City and region:</b> decides buildings, heat, transport, land use, local supply; city and county, utilities and owners. Time step: an hour to a year; horizon: to 2040 or 2050.</li><li><b>S4 Nation:</b> decides targets, policy instruments, infrastructure, security stocks, trade; national governments and regulators. Time step: representative hours to a year; horizon: decades.</li></ul>
<!-- r03-rubric:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="r3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="detail" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A more detailed model is always more accurate.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Detail adds data needs and uncertainty of its own. Match the detail to the question, and say what you left out.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="optimal" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An optimal plan predicts what will happen.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is the best plan under the model's assumptions. Real decisions and real paths depart from it, which is why a prescriptive answer comes with its limits.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="leftout" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Saying what a study leaves out makes its answer more useful, not less.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. A reader can only use an answer if they know where it holds; an unstated <span class="lx-term" data-term="system-boundary">boundary</span> invites them to use it where it does not.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>Where the defence goes next</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>In the research capstone (CR, upcoming), this design card becomes the method section of your proposal, and the mock review in CK-R asks you to defend it again. The Modeler lessons build the families in depth: <a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a> (a dispatch linear program) now, and capacity expansion, uncertainty and data analysis in the lessons to come.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Spatial resolution: zones, buses, neighbourhoods or grid cells matter as much as the time step, and are chosen the same way.</li>
<li>Coupling models: many studies link two families, for example an optimization inside a Monte Carlo loop. The “mixed” label here covers only models with a qualitative part.</li>
<li>Qualitative methods are taught at awareness level only; a fully qualitative study needs a mentor trained in them.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

</ul>
